abstract: Sex differences are prominent in neuropsychiatric, neurological, and neurodegenerative conditions. While both gonads (ovaries vs. testes) and sex chromosome complement (SCC; XX vs. XY) contribute to sex differences, these effects are hard to differentiate in humans and gonadal contributions have been considered dominant in the brain. The four core genotypes (FCG) mouse model distinguishes between SCC and gonadal effects but whether findings are conserved across species remains unclear. Here, we present the first application of the novel FCG-derived rat model to explore cell-type-specific sex differences in the medial septum (MS), which shows robust structural sex differences, and convergence/divergence between species. Differential gene expression, pathway, transcription factor, and gene regulatory network analyses show dominant SCC effects and concordant gonadal effects on gene and network regulation in rat MS cell types. Comparison between the FCG rat and mouse models find convergence across species on the dominance of the SCC in regulating gene expression in concert with gonadal effects in the MS, despite divergence in individual sex-biased genes. In both species, the sex-biased, cell-type-specific MS genes and networks are associated with diverse diseases relevant to MS functions, such as anxiety, Alzheimers Disease, epilepsy, and schizophrenia, that can be targeted by proposed therapeutic candidates. Our cross-species investigation identifies a conserved dominance of SCC effects in sex-biased gene expression in the MS, thereby challenging the classical gonad-centric view of sexual differentiation in the brain and highlighting the MS as an important region for the study of sex differences driven by the sex chromosome complement.
